doc.title: Jerry Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe and Christian Goodwillie, via Zoom, June 30, 2021

chapter: Teenage obsession and the record store
title: Opening a jazz store and learning from customers
summary: He started the store with jazz, found one-stops skeptical, expanded into R&B and funk, and learned from a mostly black clientele.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Did you get regular customers coming in who eventually would ask you your opinion?

That’s what my store was all about. When I opened the store I went to the various one- stops in the city — a one-stop is a place that carried records from all the majors. So instead of having to have an account with Polygram, an account with Warner Brothers, an account with Columbia, and often they didn’t want to give you credit as a start-up business, you could go to a one-stop, who carried records from all the companies. And I went to the one-stops, I introduced myself and I said, “Hi, I’m Jerry Gordon and I’m starting a jazz record store.” And every one said, “Are you crazy? A jazz record store? You’d better get into some other stuff because that’s not going to make it.” And there were no other jazz record stores but I was undeterred and that’s what I decided to do. And when I opened up the record store I started off with jazz records and sure enough half the people that came in started asking for non-jazz records. Okay? And I saw Jeez — you know one thing I learned from — one of the many things I learned from my father is don’t ever let a customer get away. So you know I kept jazz as the center of my concept at the record store but then I started buying R&B and funk you know, and that’s how I expanded the store. But I’m proud to say it did not take long before the customers trusted me when they saw I had jazz knowledge and asked me my opinions. I also will mention that I learned so much from my customers, you know I might have been into jazz but I was a white suburban kid and my customers were when I opened up, 75, 80 percent black and they were coming from a whole other place and I thought I knew about jazz and I realized how little I know. My best example of that, I’m sorry I’m really taking liberties with your question, the most requested record, this is to illustrate that point, the most requested record in my store in its history was Little Jimmy Scott “Falling in Love is Wonderful.”
